chapters.name: Chapter 1: Getting comfortable with your device

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Touch screen basics: tap, swipe and the home screen
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Unlock your device, open an app and get back to the home screen.
This lesson builds toward: Using your own phone or tablet, you will unlock it, use tap, swipe, press and hold and pinch, open an app and get back to the home screen, without help.
A smartphone is a phone that is also a small computer. A tablet is the same idea with a bigger screen. Most run Android (made by Google, used by Samsung, Motorola and others) or iOS and iPadOS (made by Apple for iPhone and iPad).
You control it with your finger. Tap: touch and let go, to open something. Swipe: slide your finger across, to move between pages or scroll. Press and hold: keep your finger down, to see more choices. Pinch: two fingers apart to make things bigger, together to make them smaller.
The home screen shows your apps as small pictures called icons. To go back home, swipe up from the bottom edge, or press the home button if your device has one.
Step by step:
- Press the side or top button to wake the screen.
- Swipe up and enter your code, or use your fingerprint or face.
- Tap an app icon to open it.
- Swipe up from the bottom (or press the home button) to go back home.
- Pinch two fingers apart on a photo to zoom in.
Words to know:
- Smartphone: a phone that is also a small computer with a touch screen.
- Icon: a small picture you tap to open an app.
- Home screen: the main screen that shows your apps.
- Swipe: slide your finger across the screen.
Try it now: Wake and unlock your device. Open the Camera or Weather app, swipe around, then go back to the home screen. Do it three times until it feels easy.
You can now unlock your device, open an app with a tap, scroll with a swipe and get back to the home screen.

check.q: What does press and hold do?
check.why: Keeping your finger down shows more choices.

check.q: You are in an app and want to get back to your home screen. What would you do?
options: Turn the phone off and on
Swipe up from the bottom edge, or press the home button
check.why: Swiping up from the bottom, or the home button, takes you back to the home screen.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Making it easier to see and hear
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Make the text bigger and the volume and brightness right for you.
This lesson builds toward: In the Settings app, you will change the text size, brightness and volume so the device is easy to see and hear, with each one set to a comfortable level.
You can change your device so it is easier to use. All of these are in the Settings app, which usually has a gear icon.
Bigger text: open Settings, then look for Display or Accessibility, and find text size or font size. Brightness: find it in Display, or swipe down from the top of the screen for quick controls. Volume: use the buttons on the side.
If you cannot find something, use the search box at the top of Settings and type a word like "text size". Both Android and Apple devices also have accessibility features like a magnifier and reading the screen out loud.
Step by step:
- Open the Settings app (gear icon).
- Tap the search box at the top and type "text size".
- Move the slider until the text is easy to read.
- Swipe down from the top to change brightness.
- Use the side buttons for volume.
Words to know:
- Settings: the app where you change how your device works.
- Accessibility: features that make a device easier to see, hear or touch.
Try it now: Open Settings, search for "text size" and make the text one step bigger. Then swipe down from the top and change the brightness.
You can now make text bigger and set the brightness and volume so your device is comfortable to use.

check.q: Which icon does the Settings app usually have?
check.why: Settings usually has a gear icon.

check.q: The screen is too dark to read outside. What would you do?
options: Swipe down from the top and turn up the brightness
check.why: Quick controls for brightness are found by swiping down from the top of the screen.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Calls, contacts and text messages
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Save a contact, make a call and send a text message.
This lesson builds toward: Given a person you want to reach, you will save them as a contact, call them and send them a text, and handle unknown callers safely, with the call and text sent and no codes ever given to a caller.
The Phone app makes calls. The Contacts app (on some phones it is part of the Phone app) saves names with numbers, so you can call by tapping a name instead of typing a number.
The Messages app sends text messages. Tap the new message button, choose a contact, type in the box at the bottom, and tap the send arrow.
If an unknown number calls, you can let it go to voicemail. A real caller will leave a message. Never give a code from a text message to someone who calls you.
Step by step:
- Open Contacts (or Phone, then Contacts).
- Tap the + button to add a person: name and number. Save.
- Tap the name, then the phone icon to call.
- Open Messages and tap the new message button.
- Choose the contact, type your message and tap send.
Words to know:
- Contact: a saved name and phone number.
- Text message: a short written message sent from one phone to another.
- Voicemail: a recorded message left when you do not answer.
Try it now: Save one family member or friend as a contact. Call them by tapping their name, then send them a short text: "I am practicing with my phone!"
You can now save a contact, call someone by name and send a text message.

check.why: The Messages app sends text messages.

check.q: A number you do not know calls you. What would you do?
options: Answer and give your bank details
Call back right away and read out any codes
Let it go to voicemail; a real caller will leave a message
Turn off your phone for a week
check.why: Letting unknown calls go to voicemail is safe; real callers leave a message.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Photos, apps and keeping your device safe

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Taking and sending photos
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Take a photo and send it to someone in a text.
This lesson builds toward: Using the Camera and Photos or Gallery apps, you will take a sharp photo and share it in a text with someone you know, with the photo in focus and nothing private in it.
Open the Camera app, point it at what you want, and tap the big round button. Hold the device still. Tap the screen on your subject to make it sharp.
Your photos are saved in the Photos or Gallery app. To send one, open it, tap the Share button (often a square with an arrow or three dots joined by lines), and choose Messages or email, then the person.
Think before you share. Do not send photos of your ID, bank cards, tickets with barcodes, or anything private to people you do not know.
Step by step:
- Open the Camera app.
- Point, hold still, and tap the subject to focus.
- Tap the big round button.
- Open Photos or Gallery and tap the photo.
- Tap Share, choose Messages, pick the person and send.
Words to know:
- Gallery or Photos: the app where your pictures are saved.
- Share button: the button that sends a photo or file to someone or another app.
Try it now: Take a photo of something nice near you, a plant, a meal or a view. Send it in a text to the contact you saved in Lesson 3.
You can now take a clear photo and share it with someone by text.

check.q: What does the Share button let you do with a photo?
options: Send it by text or email
check.why: Share lets you choose Messages or email and a person to send the photo to.

check.q: Your photos keep coming out blurry. What would you do?
options: Shake the phone while you take it
Hold still and tap the subject on the screen before taking it
Take it from very far away
check.why: Holding still and tapping the subject makes the photo sharp.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Installing apps safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find and install a free app from the official app store.
This lesson builds toward: In the official app store, you will find and install a free app after checking the developer, rating and reviews, and choose which permissions to allow, allowing only the permissions the app really needs.
Apps add new things your device can do: maps, the weather, video calls, your bank, your pharmacy. Get them only from the official store: the Google Play Store on Android, or the App Store on iPhone and iPad.
Search for the app by name. Before you install, check the name of the company that made it (the developer), the number of reviews, and the rating. Fake apps copy real names, so make sure it is from the real company.
When an app asks for permission to use your location, camera, contacts or microphone, ask yourself if it really needs it. A flashlight app does not need your contacts. You can say no, and change it later in Settings.
Step by step:
- Open the Play Store (Android) or App Store (Apple).
- Tap Search and type the app's name.
- Check the developer name, rating and number of reviews.
- Tap Install or Get.
- When asked for permissions, allow only what makes sense.
Words to know:
- App: a program on your phone or tablet that does one kind of job.
- Developer: the company or person who made the app.
- Permission: your OK for an app to use something like your camera or location.
Try it now: Open your official app store and install one free app that is useful to you, for example a weather app, your pharmacy's app or a bus app. Check the developer name first.
You can now find, check and install an app from the official store, and decide which permissions to allow.

check.q: Why check the developer's name before installing an app?
options: To find the app's price in a store
To change the phone's text size
Fake apps copy real names, so make sure it is from the real company
check.why: Fake apps copy real app names, so the developer name shows if it is genuine.

check.q: A game app asks for permission to use your microphone and contacts. What would you do?
options: Say no unless it really needs them; you can change it later in Settings
check.why: Only allow permissions an app really needs; you can change them later.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Keeping your device locked, updated and charged
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn on a screen lock and check for a software update.
This lesson builds toward: On your own device, you will turn on a strong screen lock, check for a software update and turn on Find My Device or Find My, with a lock that is not easy to guess and the device up to date.
A screen lock stops other people using your phone if it is lost or stolen. Use a PIN code of at least six numbers, or your fingerprint or face. Do not use 123456 or your birthday.
Updates fix security problems. Find them in Settings: on Android look for Software update or System update; on iPhone and iPad go to General, then Software Update. Plug in and use Wi-Fi when you update.
If you lose your phone, Android's Find My Device and Apple's Find My can show it on a map or lock it. Turn them on now, while you still have it.
Step by step:
- Open Settings and search for "screen lock" or "passcode".
- Set a PIN of at least six numbers, or fingerprint or face.
- Search Settings for "software update" and install any update.
- Search Settings for "Find My" and make sure it is turned on.
- Charge your device each night.
Words to know:
- PIN: a number code that unlocks your device.
- Software update: a free fix and improvement from the device maker.
- Find My Device / Find My: Android and Apple tools that help you find a lost device.
Try it now: Final task practice: check your screen lock is on, search Settings for "software update" and see if one is waiting, and turn on Find My Device or Find My. Then do the final task: call, text a fresh photo, and install one useful app.
You can now keep your device locked, up to date and findable if it is lost.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Call No call or video call was made, or the learner needed help to find the person. Calls or video-calls a saved contact without help. Also saves a new contact with a name and number first. Text with a photo The text or photo was not sent, or the photo shows private information. Takes a sharp photo and sends it in a text to someone they know. Uses the Share button from Photos or Gallery and adds a short message. Installing an app No app installed, or it came from outside the official store. One free app installed from the official store after checking the developer and reviews. Also says no to a permission the app does not need. Lock and updates No screen lock, or an easy lock such as 123456. A strong screen lock is on and software is up to date. Find My Device or Find My is also turned on. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which of these is a weak screen lock?
options: A six-number PIN that is hard to guess
check.why: 123456 or your birthday are easy to guess.

check.q: You want to be able to find your phone if you lose it. What would you do now?
options: Wait until it is lost, then look for a setting
Turn on Find My Device (Android) or Find My (Apple)
Write your PIN on the back of the phone
check.why: These tools must be turned on while you still have the phone.
